title: Three Reasons Ships Aren't Sailing Through the Strait of Hormuz Despite Trump's Announcement
summary: When President Trump announced a deal with Iran on Sunday, he ended his Truth Social post with a dramatic flourish: 'Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!' But three days later, the Strait of Hormuz—a critical chokepoint for about a fifth of the world's oil and gas—remains eerily quiet. Ship-tracking data from MarineTraffic on Tuesday shows more than 250 tankers and 330 cargo ships still huddled inside the Gulf, with many more not even broadcasting their location. So why isn't anyone moving? Experts point to three major obstacles. First, the security situation is far from stable. Since late February, Iran has fired on vessels attempting to cross without its permission. The U.S. responded with its own naval blockade of Iranian ports in April, disabling nine ships—including launching Hellfire missiles into engine rooms. Although Trump announced the 'immediate removal' of the U.S. blockade, he later said it would stay until the deal is signed. Satellite images from June 15 show four U.S. warships still near the blockade line. Second, the threat of sea mines looms large. Iran's semi-official Fars news agency reported early in the conflict that Tehran would deploy 'various types of sea mines, including floating mines' if its coastline were attacked. Both the multinational Joint Maritime Information Center and Oman's Maritime Security Centre have since issued warnings about floating objects suspected to be mines. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a Senate committee that Iran had 'mined large segments of Hormuz.' Clearing them could take anywhere from 30 days to six months, experts say. Third—and perhaps most crucially—is a profound lack of trust. Captains vividly recall April, when Iran's foreign minister declared the strait fully open, only for authorities to reverse course the next day. More than 33 vessels were forced to turn around mid-transit, and several reported being fired upon. 'What we've been seeing is still very much a wait-and-see mentality,' said Naveen Das, senior oil analyst at Kpler. 'No-one really wants to be the first to take that risk.' Some risk-tolerant Greek companies might eventually test the waters, but for now, the world's oil supply remains in a high-stakes stalemate.
why_it_matters: Even a distant conflict in the Strait of Hormuz can send shockwaves through your daily life — raising gasoline prices, disrupting the supply of goods, and reminding us how fragile global trade can be. For teenagers growing up in an interconnected world, understanding these chokepoints helps you see why peace and trust are not just abstract ideals but urgent, practical necessities.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that connects the oil‑rich Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea and the open ocean. It has been a geopolitical hotspot for decades because so much of the world’s energy supply moves through it.
Tensions over the strait are not new: in 2019, attacks on oil tankers and the shooting down of a U.S. surveillance drone brought the United States and Iran dangerously close to open conflict.

Sea mines are a cheap and effective way to threaten shipping. Clearing them is slow, dangerous work that requires specialised mine‑hunting ships and divers — and even then, some mines can drift unpredictably.
Marco Rubio, the U.S. Secretary of State under the Trump administration, played a key diplomatic role in the negotiations and testified about Iran’s mining of the strait.

Shipping companies rely on data from services like MarineTraffic and analysts at firms such as Kpler, a commodity data company, to decide when it is safe to send multi‑million‑dollar tankers through a conflict zone.

perspectives.description: If the deal holds and the sea lanes reopen, global oil prices could stabilise, benefiting economies and consumers worldwide. Diplomatic breakthroughs offer a glimpse of a future where energy security does not hang on a single narrow passage.

Shipping companies and insurers see enormous risk in trusting a region littered with mines and a history of reversals. Sending a tanker through now could mean a catastrophic loss — both human and financial — so their wait‑and‑see approach is the only rational choice.

The standoff illustrates a classic geopolitical trap: a critical chokepoint can be paralysed not just by open warfare but by the mere threat of mines and unpredictable orders. It shows that clearing physical obstacles is often faster than rebuilding trust between hostile powers.

The outcome depends on whether the U.S. and Iran can create a verifiable mechanism to guarantee safe passage, perhaps with neutral monitors. In the long run, the situation may push countries to invest in alternative routes or speed up the shift to renewable energy, reducing the world’s dependence on Hormuz entirely.
